degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: EVA thermal breakdown begins with loss of acetic acid and formation of an unsaturated polymer intermediate; further heating breaks the remaining backbone into smaller hydrocarbons. The cited photovoltaic-encapsulant study does not identify every final hydrocarbon.

Timescales: Nitrogen thermogravimetry of the studied waste-module encapsulant used 0.5–5 °C/min heating rates and found two main mass-loss stages spanning approximately 276–372 °C and 372–495 °C. These are programmed-heating results, not environmental lifetimes.

Environmental persistence: Thermal mass loss does not establish biodegradation. Crosslinking, vinyl-acetate content and the module construction limit transfer to other EVA materials.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Pyrolytic removal of EVA can enable recovery of glass and other photovoltaic-module components. The cited kinetic study supports process development for destructive delamination; it does not demonstrate recovery of reusable EVA polymer.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Heating unstabilized vinylidene-chloride polymer releases hydrogen chloride and forms a discolored, unsaturated chlorinated residue. Timescales: At 176.4 °C under flowing nitrogen, the NBS experiment follows HCl evolution over 1–24 h, with an initial induction period and a changing release rate. These are severe thermal conditions, not an outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: Neither the thermal study nor the recycling announcement measures carbon mineralization in soil or water. Discoloration, HCl release and loss of barrier function are different endpoints from complete environmental disappearance.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Solvay reports a proof of concept for recycling and reblending Ixan PVDC bi-oriented post-industrial food-packaging film while retaining high barrier performance. The public announcement does not disclose a complete process design or demonstrate routine post-consumer collection; sorting and recycling infrastructure remain separate requirements.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: ABS can undergo thermo-oxidative degradation during melt processing and heat aging, with the butadiene-rich rubber phase particularly susceptible. In a controlled study of two commercial mass- and emulsion-polymerized ABS resins melt-blended at 220 °C, processing reduced markers of the polybutadiene phase and increased yellowing; antioxidant package and production route changed the response. This is evidence for processing- and formulation-dependent stability, not a universal ABS service-life prediction.

Timescales: Repeated UVA-aging and recycling experiments show exposure- and stabilization-dependent changes; no single ABS service-life or environmental lifetime is established.

Environmental persistence: Rubber-phase oxidation and surface embrittlement are not evidence of complete mineralization.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: ABS can be mechanically recycled when the incoming stream is identified, sorted, and kept sufficiently compatible for remelting, but prior use, additives, contamination, and cumulative heat and shear history limit direct transfer of virgin-grade expectations. In one open study of black ABS recovered from rigid tablet casings, six extrusion and reinjection cycles increased melt-flow index and affected impact response while tensile, flexural, and thermal results remained broadly stable for that material set. Those outcomes apply to the named WEEE stream and process, not to all recycled ABS or mixed electronic-plastic fractions. Repeated extrusion/injection molding can redistribute damaged surface material and recover some mechanical response. Antioxidant restabilization improves thermal-oxidative resistance in the cited commercial-ABS study.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Aromatic polyester depolymerization can yield reusable acid/diol-derived products; the cited evidence specifically demonstrates PET, rather than every thermoplastic polyester.

Timescales: Milled PET-bottle material was reacted at 350 °C for 20 min in water with and without alkali.

Environmental persistence: This pressurized chemical treatment supplies no family-wide soil, marine or landfill mineralization time.
recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Reclamation depends on polyester identity and the waste stream. PET provides directly supported examples of several major routes. Industrial mechanical bottle recycling sorts, washes and dries flakes, then uses decontamination, extrusion, melt filtration and pelletizing. Chemical glycolysis yields BHET and oligomers for purification and reuse, while Eastman reports commercial methanolysis operation at Kingsport from early 2024. Laboratory hydrothermal depolymerization is another PET recovery example.

Carbios reports enzymatic PET depolymerization followed by purification of terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol at demonstration scale, with 100 packaging/textile-waste batches reported in July 2026. These PET-specific examples establish a range of recovery technologies; their catalysts, operating conditions, feedstock tolerance and commercial maturity must not be transferred to every thermoplastic polyester.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hydrolysis cleaves PET ester chains to terephthalic-acid- and ethylene-glycol-derived products; further reactions depend on treatment severity. Glycolysis with ethylene glycol instead yields BHET (bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate), dimers and oligomers. In Carbios’ enzyme-driven recovery process, the isolated monomers are terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol. These are route-qualified treatment products, not a complete inventory of ambient weathering products.

Timescales: The cited milled-bottle study used 350 °C water for 20 min, with and without KOH.

Environmental persistence: Pressurized hydrolysis demonstrates chemical conversion, not a transferable environmental mineralization time.
recyclingAndEndOfLife:
Mechanical recycling of collected PET bottles is an established industrial route: bottles are sorted, reduced to flakes, washed and dried, then decontaminated and reprocessed through extrusion, melt filtration and pelletizing. Commercial vacuum-treatment systems can also restore intrinsic viscosity. The EREMA/Texplast operating example documents this sequence; feedstock quality, decontamination and intended use determine recyclate suitability.

Chemical recovery includes glycolysis, methanolysis and hydrolysis. Glycolysis with ethylene glycol produces bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET), dimers and oligomers. A laboratory study of coloured bottles, trays and polyester textile wastes used biobased ethylene glycol and zinc acetate, followed by filtration, crystallization and activated-carbon purification. Methanolysis has reached commercial operation: Eastman reports its Kingsport polyester-renewal facility became operational in early 2024 and achieved on-spec production and revenue. The separately cited hydrothermal study demonstrates laboratory monomer-derived product recovery; solvent/catalyst management and product purification remain process-specific requirements.

Enzymatic depolymerization is another recovery route. Carbios describes pretreated PET reacting with water and an enzyme, followed by residue filtration, activated-carbon treatment and separation of terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol. Its July 2026 report documents 100 batches from packaging and textile waste at its Clermont-Ferrand demonstration plant and an expanded licensing offering. This establishes demonstration-scale operation; it does not establish widespread commercial deployment. Reactor conversion and material recycling do not imply rapid biodegradation in the environment.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: For the directly studied HBA/HNA aromatic polyester, ester cleavage recovers 4-hydroxybenzoic acid and 6-hydroxy-2-naphthoic acid or their methyl esters, depending on hydrolysis versus methanolysis. Other thermotropic LCP chemistries need separate evidence.

Timescales: Vectra fibers of 23 µm diameter, cut to about 3 mm, underwent more than 95% methanolysis in 30 h under methanol reflux with one equivalent of TBD per ester bond. At 25 °C, substantial fiber remained after 500 h.

Environmental persistence: These reagent-driven conversion rates do not establish degradation in soil or water. The study describes the difficulty of degrading wholly aromatic LC polyesters but does not determine an environmental half-life.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Superbase-assisted methanolysis and hydrolysis provide laboratory monomer recovery. TBD is consumed by association with products in this system and should not be described as a low-loading catalyst; purification is part of the route.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Batch pyrolysis of alternating ethylene/propylene/carbon-monoxide polyketone generates CO, methane, hydrogen and light hydrocarbons, with ketones, cyclopentenones, furans and aromatic compounds in the liquid fraction. Cyclization competes with chain cleavage.

Timescales: The 250 g laboratory batch was heated from ambient to above 500 °C. Strong vapor production occurred around one hour into heating, near a 400 °C reactor temperature; this is an apparatus-specific process observation.

Environmental persistence: No environmental mineralization or disappearance time follows from inert thermal decomposition.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical recycling was demonstrated for commercial aliphatic-polyketone composites containing 15 or 30 wt% short glass fiber. A 2025 study remolded fully recycled material after one and five recycling cycles; fiber and matrix changes affected retained properties. These results concern the specified composites rather than every neat polyketone grade. The study demonstrates a thermochemical conversion route to liquid, gas and solid fractions. Purification and reuse as chemical feedstock remain distinct from combustion of the gas for energy; this experiment is not evidence of established closed-loop polyketone recycling.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vacuum pyrolysis of PTFE mainly produces tetrafluoroethylene under the cited controlled conditions. Product distributions in air or poorly controlled thermal treatment may differ.

Timescales: The original study measures high-temperature volatilization kinetics, not ambient weathering.

Environmental persistence: Fluoropolymer persistence is a lifecycle concern; thermal monomer generation does not establish an environmental mineralization time.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Clean PTFE scrap is reclaimed by specialist grinding and powder routes; it cannot be processed like an ordinary low-viscosity thermoplastic melt. Pyrolytic monomer recovery is a separate specialist route.

Environmental persistence: Chemical stability and weather resistance do not supply a quantitative environmental mineralization time. FEP-specific environmental timing remains unresolved.

recyclingAndEndOfLife: The supplier directs waste to appropriate permitted treatment and does not validate a resin-recovery process. A PFA-specific reclamation route remains an evidence gap.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The Halar ECTFE guide warns of rapid thermal degradation on overheating and of accelerated damage from contamination; it does not identify the major individual degradation products.

Timescales: Its processing guidance warns against temperatures around 350 °C or above; temperature alone is not a degradation timescale or service-life prediction.

Environmental persistence: Processing stability does not establish ambient mineralization; environmental timing is not measured by the guide.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The guide describes adding less than 15% suitable regrind, with darkened or contaminated resin rejected. This is established, formulation-qualified production-scrap recovery rather than a general post-consumer route.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Selective acetolysis cleaves the PC component to acetylated bisphenol-A products while ABS can be recovered as polymer. This is controlled chemical treatment of the blend.

Timescales: A reported separation experiment uses 0.5 g PC/ABS, acetic acid and 4-pyrrolidinylpyridine at 180 °C for 2 h.

Environmental persistence: Selective PC conversion leaves ABS; neither this conversion nor blend fragmentation establishes environmental mineralization.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: A laboratory process combines organocatalyzed PC acetolysis with ABS recovery by agglomeration or dialysis, including a studied automotive part. Solvent separation and product purity are necessary; commercial adoption is not demonstrated.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The PVC backbone can lose hydrogen chloride, develop conjugated polyenes and undergo subsequent oxidation and chain breakdown. The absence of a plasticizer does not prevent backbone dehydrochlorination.

Timescales: Rates depend on stabilizers, temperature, light and product geometry; the cited lifecycle assessment does not establish one environmental lifetime for unplasticized PVC.

Environmental persistence: Aged PVC and fragments can remain after loss of additives or mechanical integrity; these changes are not complete mineralization.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Sorted unplasticized PVC can be mechanically recycled after size reduction and formulation control. The lifecycle literature also describes solvent separation and chlorine-management routes; additive composition and contamination constrain reuse.
